chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya from Ahmad ibn Muhammad and Ali ibn Ibrahim from his father, both together, from Ibn Mahboub, from Hisham ibn Salim, from Ziyad ibn Suqah, from Al-Hakam ibn Uteyba, who said:

I said to Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him): 'May Allah improve you. Indeed, some people have thirty-two teeth in their mouths, and some have twenty-eight. So upon how much is the blood-money (diyah) of the teeth divided?' He (peace be upon him) said: 'The natural creation is only twenty-eight teeth: twelve in the front of the mouth and sixteen in the back. Upon this, the blood-money of the teeth is divided.'

So the blood-money of each tooth from the front, when it breaks until it is gone, is five hundred dirhams, so the total of them is six thousand dirhams. And for each tooth from the back, when it breaks until it is gone, its blood-money is two hundred and fifty dirhams, and there are sixteen of them, so the total of them is four thousand dirhams. So the total blood-money of the front and back teeth is ten thousand dirhams.

And the blood-money was established upon this: so whatever exceeds twenty-eight teeth, there is no blood-money for it, and whatever is less, there is no blood-money for it. This is how we found it in the Book of Ali (peace be upon him).

He (the narrator) said: So Al-Hakam said: 'I said: Indeed, the blood-moneys used to be taken before today from camels, cows, and sheep.' He (peace be upon him) said: 'That was only in the villages (bedouin areas) before Islam. So when Islam became prominent and silver coins (wariq) became abundant among the people, the Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) divided it upon the silver coins.'

Al-Hakam said: So I said to him: 'What is your view of the one who is from the people of the villages today? What is taken from them regarding the blood-money today, camels or silver?' He said: 'Camels today are like silver. But they are better than silver regarding the blood-money.'

Indeed, they used to take from them regarding the accidental blood-money one hundred camels, calculated at one hundred dirhams for each camel, so that is ten thousand dirhams. I said to him: 'So what are the ages of the one hundred camels?' He said: 'Whatever a year has passed upon them, all of them males.'
ai.seo_question: What is the Islamic ruling on blood-money for teeth and how is it calculated?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Al-Kafi* establishes the jurisprudential basis for dental *diyah* by standardizing the human dentition at twenty-eight teeth, a count that reconciles natural anatomical variations within the legal framework of compensation. It highlights the historical transition from pre-Islamic livestock-based compensation to the silver-dirham standardization instituted by Imam Ali (AS), while affirming the continued validity and preference of camels for rural communities, reflecting the Shia scholarly emphasis on contextual flexibility (*siyaghah*) in applying fixed legal values.
